L'Expresse can confirm that reports stating that Prime Minister Anerood Jugnauth has passed away are correct. The 88 year old veteran politician is said to have died in his sleep on Monday night. His family was saddened by his death and were unavailable to comment.

Prime Minister Jugnauth had been involved in government since 1966 and had held a constitutional office since 1976, where he was leader of the opposition. He first served as Prime Minister in 1982 and served four terms until 1995. He was again elected for a further term between 2000 and 2003. He was then voted in as the President of Mauritius, a role in which he served until 2012 when he resigned. In 2014, he began his sixth term as Prime Minister. In this term, he continued to improve relation with countries around the world. He was also the Prime Minister responsible for the return of the Chagos Islands to Mauritian control. His last act as Prime Minister was to denounce Russia in February. In April, Jugnauth became very ill and was in and out of hospital for the next four months. Towards the back end of August, he appeared to have recovered as the hospital visits stopped. However, the illness had taken its toll and left the Prime Minister feeling tired and weak. He passed away on Monday night of natural causes.

Members of the government and the leaders of the other parties have expressed their condolences to the Jugnauth family. They praise his long career of helping Mauritius prosper and grow. Jugnauth is credited with the rapid growth of the Mauritian economy, helping the textiles business become established in the 80's. His popularity with the people of Mauritius is evidenced by the six terms he spent as Prime Minister. He was affectionately known as 'Rambo', due to him being unbeatable when it came to elections. It is expected that Deputy Prime Minister Xavier Luc Duval will take control of the country until the next election. They were scheduled for this year, but with the sudden death of the Prime Minister, all parties have agreed for the elections to take place next year instead. He will be sadly missed by all who knew him.

RIP Prime Minister Sir Anerood 'Rambo' Jugnauth, 1930-2018.

If I understand you correctly you're saying that you value the readability of code higher than algorithmic perfection. That's absolutely a sensible approach in most cases. Performance tends to be rarely a problem and if it is it tends to involve ugly hacks in small parts of the code or a change of data structures, it rarely impacts large parts of the code.

If you look at Go readability is considered so important that the language it very much designed to make it easy to write readable code, so much even that they pretty much force you into a specific code style. Python is similar (though somewhat less strict). Both are very popular languages.

I think what programmers sometimes get wrong is a mindset that quality X has to be as high as possible. In practice programming is always a trade-off between stuff like performance, correctness, time to market and long term maintainability and what matters most is that every aspect has to be good enough. Which is why many programs are written in Python, not C (performance doesn't matter enough). Which is why almost no programs are written in Coq (most programs have to be correct enough that there aren't serious bugs, they don't have to be proven perfect). Which is why software gets shipped even with bugs (a few bugs are better than a broke company). Which is why "brilliant" code is often frowned upon (if the writer goes nobody can maintain it).

But these aspects aren't independent. Readable code is often more correct. And readable code usually makes building on top of it faster. So improving readability has a positive effect on most other factors and is therefore a very good idea.

Completely agree.
